column1: 1,Explain tables EKKO and EKPO to a new joiner,"EKKO and EKPO are the two core tables behind purchase orders in SAP (the MM / Materials Management module). If you understand how they relate, most procurement reporting makes sense.
A purchase order (PO) has a header and one or more line items. SAP stores them separately:
EKKO = PO header (one row per PO)
EKPO = PO item (one row per line on the PO)
Think of a paper order form: the top section (vendor, date, company, currency) is EKKO, and the table of items below it (material, quantity, price) is EKPO.
Relationship: one EKKO record has many EKPO records, linked by the PO number EBELN.
Holds information that applies to the whole document.

column2: Document category (F = PO, K = contract, L = scheduling agreement)
Name of the person who created it

column1: Holds the details of each line.
The primary key of EKPO is EBELN + EBELP.
SELECT k.EBELN, k.LIFNR, k.BEDAT, p.EBELP, p.MATNR, p.MENGE, p.NETPR
JOIN EKPO p ON p.EBELN = k.EBELN
In ABAP this is typically an INNER JOIN on EBELN.
Where they sit in the procurement flow
Related tables you will meet quickly:
EKET: schedule lines (delivery dates and quantities per item)
EKKN: account assignment (cost center, GL account per item)
EKBE: PO history (goods receipts and invoices posted against the PO)
MARA / MAKT: material master and descriptions (join on EKPO-MATNR)
Practical tips for a new joiner
Always join EKKO and EKPO on EBELN. Never query EKPO for header attributes like vendor; those only live in EKKO.
Filter deleted items with LOEKZ = ' ' unless you specifically want them.
Check BSTYP. EKKO also stores contracts and scheduling agreements, so filter BSTYP = 'F' if you only want POs.
Use transaction SE16N or SE11 to browse the tables, and ME23N to view a PO on screen and compare it with what you see in the tables.
Open vs. delivered quantity: compare EKPO-MENGE with the totals in EKBE, or use ELIKZ to see if the item is flagged complete.
Pricing detail (conditions like discounts and freight) is not in EKPO. It lives in the condition tables (KONV / PRCD_ELEMENTS, depending on your release).

On S/4HANA, these tables still exist and work the same way, but some custom fields and views differ. Check with your team whether they report from CDS views like I_PurchaseOrderAPI01 or directly from the tables.
EKKO tells you who you’re buying from and under what terms; EKPO tells you what you’re buying, how much, and for what price.

If it would help, I can walk through a worked example with sample data, or explain EKET, EKKN and EKBE next.","You are an experienced SAP MM consultant mentoring a new joiner who has no prior SAP knowledge. For example, show how one purchase order with three materials appears as one row in EKKO and three rows in EKPO.","EKKO and EKPO: Purchase Order Data in SAP
Think of a purchase order (PO) as a paper order form. The top section (who you’re buying from, date, currency) is EKKO. The list of things you’re ordering is EKPO.
Header details are the same for the whole order, while line details differ per material. Storing the vendor once, rather than repeating it on every line, saves space and avoids inconsistencies.
EKKO: PO header (one row per PO)
EKPO: PO items (one row per line)
Both tables carry EBELN. Matching on it joins a header to its items.
The vendor and date appear once in EKKO, while each material gets its own EKPO row.
Join the two tables on EBELN, since vendor and date live only in EKKO.
Item-level data like quantity and price live only in EKPO.
Filter out deleted items (field LOEKZ) unless you need them.
EKKO holds one header row per PO (vendor, date, currency); EKPO holds one row per item (material, quantity, price).

They are linked by EBELN, so joining on it gives you the complete picture of any PO.","Act as a patient SAP MM trainer explaining to a new joiner with no SAP background, who will start pulling purchase order data for procurement reports next week. Then walk through one worked example: a PO with three materials, shown as sample rows in both tables. Add two common pitfalls (such as ignoring the deletion flag LOEKZ, or joining on the wrong key) and name two related tables, EKET and EKBE, in one line each without explaining them in depth. Structure the answer as analogy, EKKO, EKPO, example, pitfalls, then a one-line recap. Keep it under 350 words, use plain language, define any SAP term on first use, and finish with one quick question to check their understanding.","EKKO and EKPO: A Trainer’s Walkthrough

Think of a printed invoice: a cover page (who, when, which currency) and a list of line items below it. SAP stores a purchase order (PO, a formal order sent to a supplier) the same way. The cover page is EKKO, the line items are EKPO. A “table” is just a grid of rows and columns in the database.
EKKO: PO header (one row per PO)
EKPO: PO item (one row per line)
Key: EBELN + EBELP (PO number plus item number).
EKKO (1 row): 4500001234 | LIFNR 100045 | BEDAT 2026-10-15 | WAERS INR
Vendor and date appear once; each material gets its own row.
Ignoring LOEKZ. Deleted items stay in the table, so filter them out (LOEKZ blank) or your totals will be inflated.
Wrong join. Join EKKO to EKPO on EBELN only. Never match on EBELP alone, because item 00010 exists on every PO.
Two related tables you will meet later: EKET holds delivery dates per item, and EKBE holds the history of goods receipts and invoices posted against the PO.
Recap: EKKO is the PO cover page, EKPO is its line items, and EBELN links them.
Quick check: If you need the vendor name’s number for each PO item, which table does it come from, and how do you reach it?"
